text: Explain the observer pattern
expected_response: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency where a subject notifies all registered observers whenever its state changes, without knowing their concrete types. This decouples the event source from consumers and makes it easy to add or remove listeners.

text: What is the observer pattern and when should I use it?
expected_response: The observer pattern establishes a subscription mechanism where objects register interest in another object's state changes and are automatically notified. Use it when multiple objects need to react to changes in a single source without tight coupling.

text: How does the observer pattern decouple event producers from consumers?
expected_response: The subject only knows observers through a generic interface like update(). It doesn't depend on their concrete types, so producers and consumers can evolve independently. New observers can be added without modifying the subject.

text: Observer pattern for event subscriptions and notifications
expected_response: Observer lets a subject maintain a list of dependents and notify them automatically of state changes. This is the foundation of event buses, reactive streams, and data-binding frameworks. Watch for memory leaks from forgotten subscriptions.

text: Implement the observer pattern in Rust
expected_response: In Rust, define an Observer trait with an update method. The Subject stores a Vec of trait objects or function pointers. On state change, iterate and call update on each observer.

text: Observer pattern example with event listener
expected_response: An event emitter stores callback functions. When an event fires, all registered callbacks are invoked with the event data. This is observer in its simplest form: subscribe, emit, react.

text: Explain the factory pattern
expected_response: Factory Method defines an interface for creating objects but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. It isolates client code from concrete class dependencies, making it easy to extend with new product types without modifying existing code.

text: What is the factory pattern and when should I use it?
expected_response: Use Factory when the exact class to instantiate isn't known until runtime, or when you want to decouple clients from concrete implementations. It centralizes creation logic and supports the open/closed principle.

text: Explain the factory pattern using a restaurant analogy
expected_response: A restaurant menu is a factory: you order by name (burger, salad) without knowing the kitchen's recipe. The kitchen (factory) decides which chef, ingredients, and steps to use. You get a finished meal through a uniform interface (the waiter) regardless of how it was made.

text: Factory Method pattern in Python
expected_response: Define an abstract creator with a factory method. Concrete creators override it to return specific products. Client code calls the factory method without knowing which concrete class is returned.

text: Factory pattern to create objects without exposing creation logic
expected_response: Factory encapsulates the decision of which concrete class to instantiate behind a common interface. Clients request products by type or configuration, and the factory handles construction details. This keeps client code independent of specific implementations.

text: Implement factory pattern in Rust with traits
expected_response: Define a trait for the product interface. Implement concrete types. A factory function or match expression returns Box<dyn Trait> based on runtime input.

text: Explain the strategy pattern
expected_response: Strategy encapsulates a family of algorithms behind a common interface and lets the client select one at runtime. This eliminates conditional logic for algorithm selection and makes adding new strategies trivial.

text: Strategy pattern to swap algorithms at runtime
expected_response: Define a Strategy interface with a single method. Each concrete strategy implements the algorithm. The context holds a strategy reference and delegates behavior. Swapping strategies changes behavior without modifying the context.

text: What is the strategy pattern?
expected_response: Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them selectable at runtime. The context delegates algorithmic work to the current strategy, keeping algorithm selection separate from usage.

text: How does the strategy pattern differ from if-else chains?
expected_response: If-else chains embed algorithm selection in the client, making changes risky and testing hard. Strategy externalizes each algorithm into its own class, so adding or changing one requires no modification to the context or other strategies.

text: Explain the builder pattern
expected_response: Builder separates the construction of a complex object from its representation. It uses fluent method chaining to set parameters incrementally, then build() produces the final validated object. This avoids telescoping constructors and makes optional fields explicit.

text: Builder pattern in Rust for constructing configuration objects
expected_response: Rust builders use method chaining with self-consuming or &mut self setters. The build method validates and returns the final struct. Type-state builders use phantom types to enforce required fields at compile time.

text: Explain the adapter pattern
expected_response: Adapter converts the interface of an existing class into one the client expects, enabling collaboration between incompatible interfaces. It acts as a thin translation layer between two systems.

text: Adapter pattern for integrating legacy APIs
expected_response: Wrap the legacy API in an adapter that exposes the interface your code expects. The adapter translates method calls, parameter shapes, and return types. This isolates the rest of your system from the legacy interface.

text: Explain the decorator pattern
expected_response: Decorator wraps an object to add behavior dynamically without altering its interface. Decorators are stackable: logging, caching, and validation can each wrap the same service independently, avoiding subclass explosion.

text: Decorator pattern vs inheritance for extensibility
expected_response: Inheritance fixes behavior at compile time and creates combinatorial subclass explosions. Decorator adds behavior at runtime by wrapping objects, enabling flexible composition of independent features without changing the original class.

text: Design a microservices architecture
expected_response: Decompose into independently deployable services aligned with bounded contexts. Each service owns its data store and communicates via async messages or REST. Use an API Gateway for routing and an event bus for cross-service coordination.

text: How to design a microservices system
expected_response: Start by identifying bounded contexts in the domain. Each becomes a service with its own database and deployment pipeline. Use an API gateway for external access, service discovery for internal routing, and event-driven messaging for loose coupling between services.

text: Explain hexagonal architecture
expected_response: Hexagonal architecture places domain logic at the center, surrounded by ports that define how the application communicates with the outside world. Infrastructure concerns like databases and APIs are pushed to adapters on the boundary, keeping the core testable and framework-agnostic.

text: What is hexagonal architecture and ports and adapters?
expected_response: Ports and adapters (hexagonal architecture) inverts dependencies so the domain core defines interfaces (ports) that external systems implement through adapters. This keeps business logic independent of any particular framework, database, or transport.
